newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Westpac sells Fairfax stake to Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Westpac sells Fairfax stake to Merrill.

text.p: Westpac Banking Corp said on Friday that it had sold its 2.99 percent stake in newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
"Westpac has unwound its position in Fairfax," a bank spokeswoman told Reuters.
She said the 22.75 million shares were held by Westpac for trading purposes and had been sold to a broker.
United States broker Merrill Lynch specialled the shares after the market closed at A$3.30 per share, the same as Fairfax's closing price and only two cents off the record high.
Merrill Lynch said it would not make any comment on the Fairfax trading.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper said on Monday that Westpac probably bought the shares when Canadian media baron Conrad Black sold the remainder of his Fairfax shares in late March.

Black was the largest shareholder in Fairfax with a 25 percent stake but bailed out of the company in late 1996 when he failed to receive government permission to increase his stake to a level which he believed would fend off potential predators such as Kerry Packer, who has 15 percent.
Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand directly bought the bulk of the Black stake and is now the largest shareholder with a 20 percent investment.
Fairfax shareholders rejected a proposal for Brierley to be allowed to buy the other five percentage points held by Black.
The newspaper report said Brierley, which can buy three percent of a listed company every six months under local exchange rules, had its eye on the Westpac shares.
It said Brierley could trigger this share "creep provision" rule in mid-June. Brierley director Rod Price arrived in Sydney this morning but was not available for comment.

Packer, who owns the Fairfax stake through his listed Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, has been mooted by analysts as a likely bidder for the historic company once the government releases its new media policy.

The policy is expected to favour Packer and work against foreign investors by allowing television network operators such as the local billionaire to also own newspapers in the same city, which runs counter to current policy. The government has also said it was opposed to any greater concentration of foreign ownership in the media, now limited to 25 percent for newspapers and 15 percent for television stations.
Packer's son, James, said in a television interview last month that his family would like to own Fairfax by Christmas.

Fairfax, the oldest newspaper publisher in Australia which owns the Sydney Morning Herald and Melbourne Age daily broadsheets along with the Australian Financial Review business daily, is valued at A$2.50 billion based on Friday's closing price of A$3.30.
Analysts confidently believe any new owner of Fairfax would have to sell the Australian Financial Review as part of the media policy change.
The publisher of the Financial Times newspaper, Pearson Plc has expressed an interest in the local daily and its executives met last month with Australian government officials.
Other executives from its half-owned business magazine, The Economist, were also in Canberra last month.
